justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 166.2 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to 169.0 at the one-month mark. The one-day estimate is anchored primarily by recent price momentum and short-term mean reversion tendencies, assuming no major overnight catalysts. The slight upward slope in the weekly and monthly estimates reflects a general assumption of modest positive drift consistent with longer-run trend behavior, tempered by the recognition that markets rarely move in straight lines. I did not embed strong directional conviction — the point estimates are closer to a "slight continuation of recent trend" view than a bold directional call.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is consistent with how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 9.4 points, capturing typical daily volatility and the possibility of a modest surprise in either direction. By one week, that range expands to about 21 points, incorporating the possibility of shifting sentiment, macro data releases, or sector rotation. At one month, the interval widens to 42 points, reflecting the full range of plausible macro and idiosyncratic developments that could unfold — earnings, Fed communications, geopolitical developments, or broad risk-on/risk-off moves.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data or a surprise central bank policy shift, either of which could cause a sharp repricing well below the lower bound. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, an unexpected easing in financial conditions, or a relief rally from geopolitical de-escalation could push prices above the upper bound. Liquidity events or flash crashes, while rare, represent tail risks that by definition sit outside a 90% interval.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume a relatively stable volatility regime. If realized volatility spikes — as it can during periods of financial stress or sudden news shocks — the actual distribution of outcomes would have fatter tails than my stated intervals imply. Conversely, if the environment remains unusually calm, outcomes could cluster more tightly than the intervals suggest. Users should treat these intervals as reasonable probabilistic guideposts rather than hard boundaries.
